small_guidance:
- The GEMM output is 1024×8192 then row-max → reducing N=8192 to a single value per row. Current two-pass design writes a partial buffer (NUM_PID_N × M) to HBM. Try a persistent split-K-style row-max: launch grid of (num_pid_m,) where each program iterates over all N tiles, accumulating a running max across K-loops, eliminating the intermediate partial buffer and second kernel launch.
- Add larger-M autotune configs since M=1024 is small relative to N=8192. Try `BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64` and `BLOCK_M=16, BLOCK_N=512, BLOCK_K=32` so each program reduces a wider slice of N per pass, lowering the number of partials per row.
- Preload `weight.t()` once at init (store as `[K, N]` contiguous) so the inner loop loads B contiguously along N, removing the strided W access pattern.
large_guidance:
- Restructure as a single persistent kernel: one program per row-block of M, looping internally over all N tiles, accumulating both `tl.dot` and a running scalar max per row. This eliminates the partial buffer, second kernel launch, and grid-level reduction — the (x-mean)/GELU epilogue (which on a (B,1) tensor is identically zero) folds trivially into the final store.
- Alternative split-K layout: since N=K=8192 and M=1024, treat the GEMM as a tall-skinny problem and use a streamK-style 1D grid where each program owns a contiguous strip of N for a single row block, using atomicMax (on int-reinterpreted floats) into a per-row scalar to avoid the partial materialization.
- Consider keeping weight pre-transposed as a model buffer in `__init__` (one-time cost) so the hot kernel always sees the K-contiguous layout — current `weight.contiguous().cuda()` on every forward is wasteful and the transpose-in-kernel via strided loads costs L2 bandwidth.
